title: Provable Cross-Modal Transfer of Hierarchical Concept Structure in CLIP Embeddings
claim: Contrastive pairing with hierarchical co-occurrence pulls text embeddings toward subtree means, so they inherit the image prototypes' hierarchical geometry.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid, clockwise flow, matching geometry in first and last
description: A 2x2 grid of panels explains how hierarchy moves from image to text embeddings. Top-left shows image prototypes as colored dots (blue for dog, red for cat) fanning out from a purple root, mu_animal. Dotted blue and red lines mark the subtree boundaries, and an angle inequality sits underneath. Top-right shows a labrador photo with solid and dashed arrows to the text boxes labrador, dog and animal, which stand for paired and unpaired captions. Bottom-left shows two dog photos, a labrador and a corgi, with arrows to the text box dog. An averaging formula shows that the mean of the paired images approaches mu_dog. Bottom-right repeats the top-left geometry for text embeddings a_k, with a proportionality formula and the same angle inequality. The eye starts at the top-left cluster and the mirrored bottom-right cluster.
caption: How contrastive learning transfers hierarchy from image to text embeddings. Top-left: the image prototypes are arranged so that each concept is closer to its descendants than to concepts in other subtrees. The blue and red dotted lines indicate the boundary of the dog and cat subtrees, respectively. Top-right: each image of a labrador is a variation of the labrador prototype, and its caption may pair with any concept on the path from the root to that leaf, so an image can be captioned labrador, dog or animal. Bottom-left: the pairing also means that the caption dog pairs with images of dog or any of its descendants, so the average of these images approaches the mean of the dog subtree. Bottom-right: contrastive learning pulls each text embedding toward the corresponding subtree mean, so the text embeddings inherit the arrangement of the image prototypes.
abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, not to represent taxonomies. Yet empirical studies show that CLIP embeddings exhibit hierarchical structure aligned with the hierarchy of semantic concepts. A theoretical characterization of why such hierarchy emerges from a non-hierarchical objective remains open. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), a geometric property whereby each non-leaf concept embedding is more similar to its descendants than to off-branch concepts. Empirically, we show that HAS holds approximately in raw images and randomly initialized CLIP image embeddings, while in text embeddings it holds approximately only after contrastive learning. To theoretically explain this asymmetry, we analyze an unconstrained features model in which the image embeddings are fixed and only the text embeddings are trained. At the global minimizer, the text-side HAS violation percentage at each node is at most the image-side HAS violation and near-violation percentage. The key mechanism is the hierarchical co-occurrence structure of image-text pairs, which biases text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. For a linear contrastive loss, we derive a closed-form solution that makes this mechanism explicit. We extend the analysis to the InfoNCE loss and establish analogous guarantees under sufficient regularization. Synthetic experiments validate the theory and show that HAS is transferred even beyond the regimes covered by our analysis.
